claims.text: Premelting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is initiated by surface segregation of Cu.
Cu is the lowest-melting component of the Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu alloy.
Surface-segregated Cu locally depresses the melting temperature.
Differences in elemental cohesive energies and surface energies drive Cu segregation.
Cu segregation creates a liquid-like surface layer that enables progressive melting below the expected bulk melting point.
The initial 5–15 nm Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are crystallized solid solutions with a uniform distribution of all five elements.
Heating causes localized surface Cu enrichment through atomic diffusion driven by surface-energy minimization.
Cu has lower cohesive energy than the other relevant alloy components and therefore preferentially segregates to the nanoparticle surface upon heating.
The Cu-enriched surface becomes locally liquefied while the alloy core remains solid at a higher temperature.
Melting initiates at the nanoparticle surface and progresses inward.
STEM-EDS will show increasing surface Cu enrichment as Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles approach premelting.
Surface Cu enrichment will coincide with surface roughening and localized liquid-like regions.
Cu-depleted Fe–Ni–Cr–Co control nanoparticles will require a higher temperature than Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles to develop similar premelting features.
Cu-depleted Fe–Ni–Cr–Co nanoparticles will retain a more homogeneous elemental distribution until near-complete melting.
High configurational entropy in a uniformly mixed high-entropy alloy delays melting.
In the absence of segregation, the nanoparticles would melt more uniformly and closer to the bulk-alloy melting temperature.
The proposed mechanism applies to approximately 5–15 nm nanoparticles under high vacuum during controlled thermal ramping.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to much larger particles or environments that substantially alter surface-energy effects.
